newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Manuel defends credit rating record.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Manuel defends credit rating record.

text.p: Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Wednesday rejected opposition allegations that rising crime and violence and opposition to government economic policies would affect South Africa's credit rating.

During a mini-debate in parliament, several National Party MPs alleged that South Africa's international image had slumped over the last six months and this could affect the government's ability to borrow abroad.

Manuel rejected this as politicking and said that several recent bond issues as well as credit ratings announced by lead agencies such as Moody's Investor Service (BAA3), Standard & Poor's (BB+) and Nippon Investors Service Inc (BBB) indicated that South Africa was well regarded.

Each rating granted involved an in-depth analysis of a country's economic and political risks and in South Africa's case its past and the debt standstill under apartheid had also been taken into account.
"The Yankee issue is trading exceedingly successfully...at about 160 basis points above the equivalent US Treasury bonds," Manuel said.
"There are very few countries in the world that can compare with that. The spread has not widened and we have nothing to fear in those markets.
"Very importantly as well is that, in respect of the Japanese Bond Research Institute, South Africa is ranked 33 out of 98 countries according to country risk ranking."
It was rated ahead of such countries as Israel, Hungary, China and Columbia.
"Investor sentiment will be determined by the market," Manuel said.
"We have done issues in the Samurai, Euro, Bulldog and Yankee markets and all of those have been very good, long-term issues and I do not think that we have much to fear.
"We have got to stop talking this economy down by our own pessimism about the result of the elections in 1994," Manuel added.
